sections.heading: Amazon EFS gives many Linux clients one shared file system over NFS

plan.problem: Several instances need the same files at the same time. A volume belongs to one instance, and a bucket needs API calls; a file system gives every client the same folders.
trace: **Keep files in folders.** File storage keeps data in a [hierarchical structure of files and folders] (efs-decision-guide-definition-file-storage), and Amazon EFS is a [file storage service] (efs-faq-use-case-file-vs-block-vs-object).

**Mount over NFS.** Clients speak the [Network File System version 4] protocol in the versions [NFSv4.1 and NFSv4.0] (efs-protocol-nfsv4-versions); using EFS with [Microsoft Windows–based Amazon EC2 instances] [is not supported] (efs-windows-ec2-not-supported).

**Share it widely.** Clients use it [concurrently from multiple NFS clients] in several Availability Zones (efs-concurrent-access-multiple-clients-multiple-azs): [Amazon EC2, Amazon ECS, Amazon EKS] and [AWS Lambda, and AWS Fargate] (efs-compute-services-ec2-ecs-eks-lambda-fargate).

**Plan no capacity.** EFS is [serverless, fully elastic file storage] that grows and shrinks [without provisioning or managing storage capacity] (efs-serverless-elastic-no-provisioning), up to [petabytes] (efs-faq-store-petabytes).
plan.table: Who can mount it (columns: Client | Can it mount EFS? | How): Linux instance | yes | NFS or the EFS mount helper (subsection 2); Windows instance | no: [is not supported] (efs-windows-ec2-not-supported) | use FSx for Windows File Server (subsection 9); ECS or Fargate task | yes, [both EC2 and Fargate launch types] (efs-faq-access-from-ecs-task-definition) | a volume in the task definition; Lambda function | yes | [an EFS file system in your function settings] (efs-faq-access-from-lambda-function-settings); server on premises | yes, Linux | over Direct Connect or VPN (subsection 2).
plan.why: Why a file system and not a shared disk? Each client keeps the normal file interface, with [strong consistency and file locking] (efs-faq-efs-semantics-strong-consistency-locking), so an application that writes to a directory [requires no changes to your existing applications] (efs-overview-regional-linux-shared-access).
plan.exam_signal: "shared file system for Linux instances" or "a directory that many instances read and write" points to Amazon EFS ([concurrently from multiple NFS clients], efs-concurrent-access-multiple-clients-multiple-azs); "Windows" or "SMB" points away from EFS ([is not supported], efs-windows-ec2-not-supported), to FSx for Windows File Server.
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: AWS positions EFS as [primary storage] for data that originates in the file system, and S3 Files for data that already lives in Amazon S3 ([you already have data in S3], s3-files-vs-efs-vs-fsx; S3 Files is [Built using Amazon EFS] (s3-files-built-on-efs-data-stays-in-s3), lowercase 'built'). Both s3-files facts are volatile (launch 2026-04-07): prose only, never a question key. Reference only: close-to-open consistency, advisory locking ([only supports advisory locking], efs-advisory-locking-only), the single-file maximum [47.9 TiB] (efs-limit-single-file-size; B-list), Fargate platform version, EKS CSI driver.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: EFS is one shared folder that many Linux clients mount at once. The thing to watch is Windows clients.
plan.stop_and_answer: A Lambda function and three Fargate tasks must read the same 2 GB model file and write results next to it. Can they share one EFS file system? Answer: yes; Lambda references [an EFS file system in your function settings] (efs-faq-access-from-lambda-function-settings), and ECS tasks reference it in the task definition with [both EC2 and Fargate launch types] (efs-faq-access-from-ecs-task-definition). The 2 GB is an example value in the prompt.

sections.heading: Each client reaches EFS through the mount target in its own Availability Zone

plan.problem: An instance in one zone cannot use a disk in another zone, but it can reach a network address. EFS gives each zone its own address for the same file system.
trace: **Create a mount target in each zone.** A mount target [provides an IP address for an NFSv4 endpoint] (efs-mount-target-definition-ip-nfs-endpoint); you create [one mount target in each Availability Zone], and the instances of that zone [share that mount target] (efs-one-mount-target-per-az-shared-by-instances).

**Mount by DNS name.** The file system's [Domain Name Service (DNS) name] [resolves to the IP address of the EFS] mount target in the instance's own zone (efs-dns-name-resolves-to-same-az-mount-target); AWS recommends that you [use the EFS mount helper] (efs-mount-helper-recommended-nfs-alternative).

**Open the NFS port.** A client mounts only if it reaches the [NFS port (TCP port 2049)] of a mount target (efs-nfs-client-needs-network-connection-to-port-2049), through the [security groups for the EFS mount targets] (efs-security-groups-on-mount-target-and-instance).

**Stay in one VPC.** A file system has mount targets in [only one VPC at a time] (efs-mount-targets-only-one-vpc-at-a-time); servers on premises connect over [AWS Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN] (efs-onpremises-mount-via-direct-connect-or-vpn).
plan.table: Who connects, and how (columns: Client | Path | What to watch): instance in a zone with a mount target | that zone's mount target | access [within the same Availability Zone] [for performance and cost reasons] (efs-regional-mount-target-per-az-same-az-access); Lambda function | its VPC subnets | [a mount target in every Availability Zone] that the function uses (lambda-efs-mount-target-every-az); Linux server on premises | Direct Connect or VPN | a [mount target IP address instead of] the DNS name (efs-onpremises-use-mount-target-ip-instead-of-dns), and an inbound rule for the [NFS port (2049)] (efs-onpremises-security-group-allow-nfs-port-2049); instance in another VPC or account | peering or a transit gateway | [resolve the EFS mount target manually] (efs-other-account-or-vpc-resolve-mount-target-manually).
plan.why: Why one mount target per zone? Mount targets are [designed to be highly available] inside their zone (efs-mount-targets-highly-available-static-ip-dns), and a client that uses its own zone's target pays [no data transfer charges] for that access (efs-pricing-no-charge-same-az-access).
plan.exam_signal: "on-premises servers must mount the file system" points to Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN plus an inbound NFS rule ([AWS Direct Connect or Site-to-Site VPN], efs-onpremises-mount-via-direct-connect-or-vpn); "instances in a new Availability Zone" points to a new mount target in that zone ([one mount target in each Availability Zone], efs-one-mount-target-per-az-shared-by-instances).
plan.spot_the_bug: Spot the bug prompt: a team creates mount targets in three zones. The mount targets' security group allows inbound HTTPS from the web instances' security group, and every mount command hangs. What is wrong? Reveal: an NFS client [can only mount a file system] if it reaches the [NFS port (TCP port 2049)] of a mount target (efs-nfs-client-needs-network-connection-to-port-2049); allow TCP 2049 from the instances' security group instead of HTTPS. About 60 words with the reveal.
plan.startup_example: Startup example callout, story only, at most 25 words with the label, number from uses_numbers (availability_zones_used: 3 at stage 2): 'Callvale creates one mount target in each of its three Availability Zones, so every web instance and every worker mounts through its own zone.' The story states no AWS rule; the trace carries the facts.
plan.body_extras: Reference only (B-list or nothing): [1,400 mount targets] per VPC (efs-quota-mount-targets-per-vpc), [5 security groups] per mount target (efs-quota-security-groups-per-mount-target), connections per file system, the Region property for a cross-Region mount, DataSync and AWS Transfer Family for moving data (chapter 25: <!-- xref: 25 DataSync and Transfer Family -->). Do not state a file-system count per account (brief.v0 d136).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: each zone gets one mount target, and clients use their own. The thing to watch is the NFS port in the security group.
plan.stop_and_answer: A company connects its data center to the VPC with Site-to-Site VPN. An on-premises Linux server still cannot mount the file system by its DNS name. Name two changes. Answer: mount by a [mount target IP address instead of] the DNS name (efs-onpremises-use-mount-target-ip-instead-of-dns), and add an inbound rule for the [NFS port (2049)] from the server's address range to the mount target security group (efs-onpremises-security-group-allow-nfs-port-2049).

sections.heading: A Regional file system survives a zone failure but One Zone does not

plan.problem: A file system that lives in one zone stops when that zone stops. Production files need copies in several zones; test files that can be rebuilt may not.
trace: **Choose the type at creation.** [Regional file systems (recommended)] store data across [multiple geographically separated Availability Zones] (efs-regional-recommended-type).
**Regional keeps serving.** A Regional file system gives [continuous availability to the data] when zones are unavailable (efs-regional-multi-az-continuous-availability).

**One Zone stays in one zone.** One Zone file systems [store data redundantly within a single AZ] (efs-faq-one-zone-single-az) and are [not resilient to a complete AZ outage] (efs-onezone-not-resilient-to-az-outage).

**One mount target.** One Zone has [only one highly available EFS mount target] (efs-faq-one-zone-single-mount-target); clients in that zone [avoid data transfer charges between Availability Zones] (efs-onezone-same-az-avoids-transfer-charges-better-performance).
plan.table: Regional or One Zone (columns: Question | Regional | One Zone): where data is stored | [multiple geographically separated Availability Zones] (efs-regional-recommended-type) | [store data redundantly within a single AZ] (efs-faq-one-zone-single-az); loss of a zone | designed to [sustain data if an AZ is lost] (efs-regional-designed-to-sustain-az-loss) | [file systems might be lost] (efs-whatisefs-one-zone-single-az-loss-risk); mount targets | one in each zone | [only one highly available EFS mount target] (efs-faq-one-zone-single-mount-target); SLA uptime level | [99.99%] (efs-sla-monthly-uptime-standard-99-99) | [99.9%] (efs-sla-monthly-uptime-one-zone-99-9); fits | production files | [development, build, and staging environments] (efs-faq-one-zone-use-cases).
plan.why: Why offer One Zone at all? Many workloads [do not require the Multi-AZ availability and durability] of Regional file systems (efs-pricing-one-zone-for-no-multi-az-need), so they trade zone resilience for a lower bill. Write no percentage: no saved page gives one (brief.v0 d016).
plan.exam_signal: "development, test or staging", "the data can be re-created" and "MOST cost-effective" point to One Zone ([development, build, and staging environments], efs-faq-one-zone-use-cases); "must remain available if an Availability Zone fails" points to Regional ([continuous availability to the data], efs-regional-multi-az-continuous-availability).
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: One Zone file systems are backed up by default ([enabled by default for all EFS One Zone], efs-backup-onezone-enabled-by-default-faq), and a backup can be restored to a [different AWS Region] (efs-onezone-automatic-backup-aws-backup). Reference only: ECS and Lambda must use [subnets that are in the same Availability Zone] (efs-onezone-ecs-eks-lambda-same-az-subnets), the Availability Zone name in the mount command, durability [99.999999999%] (efs-faq-durability-11-nines; B-list), One Zone throughput maxima, the free tier.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Regional survives a zone loss and One Zone does not. The thing to watch is data that you cannot rebuild.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team keeps nightly build artifacts on a One Zone file system in AZ 1, and its build servers run in AZ 1 and AZ 2. Which servers pay to reach the files, and what happens to the artifacts if AZ 1 fails? Answer: the AZ 2 servers cross zones, while AZ 1 servers [avoid data transfer charges between Availability Zones] (efs-onezone-same-az-avoids-transfer-charges-better-performance); if AZ 1 fails, the data is unavailable and [file systems might be lost] (efs-whatisefs-one-zone-single-az-loss-risk), so the team rebuilds the artifacts or restores a backup.

sections.heading: Elastic throughput follows the workload and Provisioned throughput follows your setting

plan.problem: Some applications read in short, sharp spikes; others read at a steady, known rate all day. Paying for the peak all day wastes money in the first case.
trace: **Three modes.** EFS offers [three throughput modes] (efs-three-throughput-modes): [Elastic, Provisioned, and Bursting].

**Elastic follows demand.** Elastic is the [default throughput mode in the Amazon EFS console] and [recommended for most use cases] (efs-elastic-throughput-default-recommended); it [scales automatically], and you [pay only for the amount of metadata] and data that you read or write (efs-elastic-scales-automatically-no-provisioning-pay-per-use).

**Provisioned follows your setting.** [you specify a level of throughput] [independent of the file system's size] (efs-provisioned-throughput-independent-of-size), and you are [charged for the amount of throughput enabled] (efs-provisioned-billed-for-throughput-enabled).

**Bursting follows size.** Bursting gives throughput that [scales with the amount of storage] (efs-throughput-bursting-scales-with-storage); [Burst credits accrue] below the base rate and are [deducted when throughput exceeds the base rate] (efs-bursting-credits-accrue-below-base-and-deducted-above).
plan.table: Which mode (columns: Workload | Mode | Why): spiky or unpredictable, averaging [5% or less of the peak throughput] (efs-elastic-best-for-spiky-low-average-to-peak) | Elastic | pay for what you use; known and steady, [5% or more of the average-to-peak ratio] (efs-provisioned-use-when-known-needs-5-percent-or-more) | Provisioned | pay for a set level; throughput that should grow with the data stored | Bursting | it [scales with the amount of storage] (efs-throughput-bursting-scales-with-storage); Bursting at [more than 80% of the permitted throughput] or out of credits (efs-throughput-bursting-constrained-move-to-elastic-or-provisioned) | Elastic or Provisioned | the file system is throughput-constrained.
plan.why: Why three modes? A steady workload pays least for a fixed level, and a spiky one pays least per use. You can [change the throughput mode], and it [does not cause application downtime] (efs-switch-throughput-mode-no-downtime).
plan.exam_signal: "spiky", "unpredictable" or "unknown peak throughput" points to Elastic ([spiky or unpredictable workloads], efs-elastic-best-for-spiky-low-average-to-peak); "predictable, sustained high throughput" points to Provisioned ([predictable and high levels of sustained throughput requirements], efs-pricing-provisioned-throughput-predictable-sustained).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: Bursting credits and Max I/O. Bursting gives a base of [50 KiBps per each GiB] (efs-bursting-base-rate-per-gib) and bursts to [100 MiBps per TiB] with credits (efs-bursting-burst-rate-with-credits). Max I/O has [higher per-operation latencies with Max I/O] (efs-general-purpose-always-recommended-max-io-higher-latency) and is [not supported for One Zone file systems] and for [file systems that use Elastic throughput] (efs-max-io-not-supported-one-zone-or-elastic); you [cannot change the performance mode] later (efs-performance-mode-cannot-change-after-available). At most 70 words.
plan.body_extras: One clause may say that Elastic replaced Bursting as the default on [2023-04-13] (efs-change-elastic-replaces-bursting-default-2023-04; Changed recently in 1-fast.md). Reference only: after a switch to Provisioned you [wait at least 24 hours] before you switch again (efs-provisioned-24-hour-wait-before-switch-or-decrease; B-list), per-client limits ([1,500 mebibytes per second], efs-limit-nfs-client-throughput-elastic; B-list), default Elastic IOPS, read metering, Region maxima. Never state the Elastic Region maxima: their values changed in 2025 (volatile change facts). Do not link the display 'we recommend using the default modes' (says 'we').
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Elastic for spikes and Provisioned for a steady known rate. The thing to watch is Bursting, which ties speed to size.
plan.stop_and_answer: A file system stores 50 GiB, and a nightly job reads it at a steady high rate for six hours. On Bursting it runs out of credits every night. Which mode fits a known, steady need? Answer: Provisioned throughput, because [you specify a level of throughput] [independent of the file system's size] (efs-provisioned-throughput-independent-of-size); AWS suggests it when you [know your workload's performance requirements] (efs-provisioned-use-when-known-needs-5-percent-or-more). Elastic also works and bills per use. The values are example values in the prompt.

sections.heading: Cold files move to cheaper classes and stay there unless you ask

plan.problem: Most files are hot for a few weeks and then rarely read. Keeping them in the fastest class all year pays for speed that nobody uses.
trace: **New data lands in Standard.** New data is [first written to the EFS Standard storage class] (efs-standard-class-ssd-lowest-latency-new-data-first), which has [sub-millisecond latencies] (efs-faq-standard-sub-millisecond).

**A policy moves cold files.** Lifecycle management can [automatically transition data between storage classes] (efs-lifecycle-automatic-transition-between-classes); the recommended policy moves a file after [30 days] to IA (efs-lifecycle-default-ia-after-30-days) and after [90 days] to Archive (efs-lifecycle-default-archive-after-90-days), counted from when it was [last accessed in the Standard storage class] (efs-lifecycle-transition-based-on-last-access-timer-reset).

**Cheaper, with a slower first byte.** EFS IA suits files read [a few times a quarter], EFS Archive files read [a few times a year or less] (efs-faq-ia-quarter-archive-year-designed-for); IA offers [up to 95% lower cost] than Standard (efs-faq-ia-cost-95-percent).

**They stay cold.** By default, read files are [not moved back to the Standard storage class] (efs-lifecycle-default-no-move-back-to-standard); a Transition into Standard policy can [transition files into Standard storage] on first access (efs-lifecycle-transition-to-standard-on-first-access).
plan.table: Three classes (columns: Class | Read how often | First-byte latency | Watch): EFS Standard | often | [sub-millisecond latencies] (efs-faq-standard-sub-millisecond) | the highest storage price; EFS IA | [a few times a quarter] (efs-faq-ia-quarter-archive-year-designed-for) | [tens of milliseconds] (efs-latency-ia-archive-first-byte) | files [smaller than 128 KiB] are billed as 128 KiB (efs-faq-ia-archive-128-kib-billing); EFS Archive | [a few times a year or less] | [tens of milliseconds] | a [minimum storage duration of 90 days] (efs-faq-archive-minimum-duration-90-days), and it needs Elastic throughput ([supported on EFS file systems with Elastic throughput], efs-archive-needs-elastic-throughput-no-bursting-provisioned).
plan.why: Why not move everything to IA? You pay storage per class and are [billed data access charges] when IA or Archive files are read (efs-ia-archive-billed-per-class-plus-access-charges), so a cheaper class pays off only for files that stay cold.
plan.exam_signal: "files are rarely accessed after 30 days" with "MOST cost-effective" points to a lifecycle policy to EFS IA ([a few times a quarter], efs-faq-ia-quarter-archive-year-designed-for); "unpredictable access, fast reads when a file is used again" points to Transition into Standard on first access ([back to EFS Standard when they are accessed], efs-faq-intelligent-tiering-promotes).
plan.diagram: efs-fsx-lifecycle (timeline), after the table; caption and alt fixed in diagrams below; no numbered steps.
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: file metadata is [always stored in Standard] (efs-metadata-always-stored-in-standard), and [listing the contents of a directory] does not count as file access (efs-metadata-operations-do-not-count-as-access). Reference only: the valid lifecycle values, Archive at [up to 50% lower cost] than IA (efs-faq-archive-cost-50-percent), writes to IA files going to Standard first, 128 KiB metering increments, no access charges for AWS Backup.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: a lifecycle policy moves cold files to cheaper classes. The thing to watch is the setting that brings them back.
plan.stop_and_answer: A legal team opens contracts often in their first month, then almost never, but sometimes reopens an old contract every day for a week. Which two lifecycle settings fit? Answer: move files to IA after [30 days] (efs-lifecycle-default-ia-after-30-days), and transition them back to Standard on first access, for the [fastest latency performance] (efs-lifecycle-transition-to-standard-on-first-access).

sections.heading: Security groups decide who connects and IAM policies decide who mounts

plan.problem: A file system is shared by design, so three questions decide access: who may connect, who may mount, and what each user may touch. EFS answers each with a different control.
trace: **The network lets clients connect.** [network security policies, such as security groups] on the mount targets decide which clients reach the file system (efs-security-access-iam-and-security-groups).

**IAM decides who mounts.** A file system policy can [control which clients can mount your file system] (efs-faq-file-system-policy-mount-permissions) and grant [read-only, write, and root access] (efs-iam-identity-and-resource-policies-control-client-access); for IAM authorization you [must use the EFS mount helper] (efs-iam-nfs-client-authorization-requires-mount-helper).

**POSIX decides files.** Inside, [Portable Operating System Interface (POSIX) permissions] apply (efs-posix-permissions-and-no-code-change-for-nfs-apps); an access point can [enforce a user identity] and [enforce a different root directory] (efs-access-point-enforces-posix-user-and-root-directory).

**Encrypt at rest and in transit.** You [enable encryption at rest when creating] the file system and [enable encryption in transit when you mount] it (efs-two-forms-encryption-when-enabled), with [Transport Layer Security (TLS) 1.2] (efs-faq-encryption-in-transit-tls-1-2).
plan.table: Four layers (columns: Layer | Control | Question it answers): network | security groups on the mount targets (efs-security-groups-on-mount-target-and-instance) | can the client reach the [NFS port (TCP port 2049)] (efs-nfs-client-needs-network-connection-to-port-2049)?; identity | file system policy and IAM | may this client mount, read or write?; files | POSIX permissions and access points | which user and which directory?; data | AWS KMS keys and TLS ([Encryption keys are managed by the AWS KMS], efs-faq-encryption-at-rest-kms) | is the data encrypted at rest and in transit?
plan.why: Why so many layers? The default file system policy [does not use IAM to authenticate] and [grants full access to any anonymous client] that can reach a mount target (efs-default-file-system-policy-full-access-anonymous), so until you add a policy, the network is the only lock.
plan.exam_signal: "each application must see only its own directory" points to an EFS access point ([enforce a different root directory], efs-access-point-enforces-posix-user-and-root-directory); "encrypt data in transit to the file system" points to the mount helper's TLS option ([establishes a secure TLS connection], efs-mount-helper-tls-option-encrypts-nfs-traffic).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: access points for many applications. An access point is [a network endpoint] (efs-faq-access-point-definition) that sets an [operating system user and group] and [a root directory for all connections] (efs-access-point-faq-configure-os-user-group-root-directory); an IAM policy can make [specific applications use a specific access point] (efs-access-point-iam-policy-enforces-specific-access-point). You still [create at least one mount target] first (efs-access-point-needs-mount-target-first). Lambda functions need matching execution-role permissions (lambda-efs-role-permissions). At most 70 words.
plan.body_extras: One clause only, because the fast trap list teaches it: you [cannot change its encryption setting] after creation (efs-encryption-setting-cannot-change-after-creation). Do not link the display 'you must explicity enable encryption' (AWS's misspelling); say that the AWS CLI and API need encryption turned on explicitly and link [encryption at rest is enabled by default] in the console (efs-encryption-at-rest-console-default-cli-explicit). Reference only: Block Public Access, CloudTrail logging of IAM decisions, SCP enforcement, the group-ID limit.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: security groups let clients connect, and IAM lets them mount. The thing to watch is the open default policy.
plan.stop_and_answer: Two teams share one file system. Team A must see only /team-a and must act as one fixed Linux user, whatever user its instances run as. What do you create? Answer: an access point for team A, which can [enforce a user identity] and [enforce a different root directory] (efs-access-point-enforces-posix-user-and-root-directory), plus an IAM policy so that team A's role mounts only through it ([specific applications use a specific access point], efs-access-point-iam-policy-enforces-specific-access-point).

sections.heading: EFS Replication keeps a read-only copy in another Region or zone

plan.problem: A Regional file system survives the loss of a zone, not the loss of a Region or a folder deleted by mistake. Disaster recovery needs a copy elsewhere, and mistakes need a copy from the past.
trace: **Replicate continuously.** EFS Replication [automatically and transparently replicates] data and metadata (efs-replication-automatic-transparent-data-and-metadata) to a [Region or Availability Zone (AZ) of your choice] (efs-replication-destination-faq-region-or-az-of-choice), sending [only incremental changes] (efs-replication-destination-new-or-existing-region-of-choice).
**The replica is read-only.** While replication runs, the destination is a [new read-only destination file system] (efs-replication-destination-read-only-while-replicating).

**Recover in minutes.** Replication is designed for an [objective (RTO) of minutes] (efs-replication-rpo-rto-minutes), and for most file systems it keeps an RPO of 15 minutes (efs-replication-rpo-15-minutes-most-file-systems: link the display '15 minutes' requested as fr-0098; until it is filled write the number with <!-- needs-display: efs-replication-rpo-15-minutes-most-file-systems "15 minutes" -->, never with the display 'RPO) of 15 minutes').
**Fail over by deleting the link.** You fail over [by deleting its replication configuration]; then [the replica becomes writeable] (efs-replication-failover-delete-configuration-replica-writeable).

**Back up for the past.** In the console, [automatic backups are turned on by default] (efs-backup-on-by-default-in-console), with [daily backups with a 35-day retention period] (efs-default-backup-plan-daily-35-day-retention).
plan.table: Replication or backup (columns: Question | EFS Replication | AWS Backup): what it is for | a current copy for a zone or Region disaster | older copies for deletes and mistakes; how fresh | an RPO of 15 minutes for most file systems (fr-0098) | [daily backups with a 35-day retention period] by default (efs-default-backup-plan-daily-35-day-retention); when the copy is usable | read-only until you fail over | after a [full restore or an item-level restore] (efs-backup-restore-new-or-existing-full-or-item-level); how it copies | [only incremental changes] (efs-replication-destination-new-or-existing-region-of-choice) | [incremental backups of EFS file systems] (efs-backup-incremental-and-restore-to-standard).
plan.why: Why keep both? Replication holds only the current state, for a fast failover; AWS Backup keeps restore points from earlier days, which a [full restore or an item-level restore] can bring back (efs-backup-restore-new-or-existing-full-or-item-level).
plan.exam_signal: "an RPO and RTO of minutes in another Region" for EFS points to EFS Replication ([objective (RTO) of minutes], efs-replication-rpo-rto-minutes); "restore files that were deleted last week" points to AWS Backup ([full restore or an item-level restore], efs-backup-restore-new-or-existing-full-or-item-level).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: what the replica lacks. EFS [does not create any mount targets] on the destination (efs-replication-destination-has-no-mount-targets), so create them before a failover. Data is readable [only after the initial sync completes] (efs-replication-initial-sync-before-replica-accessible), and replication is not done in a [point-in-time consistent manner] (efs-replication-not-point-in-time-consistent). Failback works by [transferring only incremental changes] (efs-faq-failback-incremental-changes). You can also [replicate EFS file systems across AWS accounts] (efs-cross-account-replication-supported). At most 70 words.
plan.body_extras: Reference only: replica lifecycle savings [up to 92%] (efs-faq-replication-replica-lifecycle-savings-92), the TimeSinceLastSync metric, billing for both file systems, about 12 MiB of hidden metered data on the destination, one replication configuration per file system, and that a file system in a configuration cannot be deleted (Try it efs-fsx-t03 shows it). AWS Backup in depth is chapter 24 (<!-- xref: 24 AWS Backup plans and vaults -->). The cross-account replication change (2024-11-19) has no changed record: teach it as current truth, never as a question key.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: replication keeps a read-only copy that you can promote in minutes. The thing to watch is older versions, which need backups.
plan.stop_and_answer: During a Region outage, an application in the second Region mounts the replica, and every write fails. What step was missed, and what else must exist there? Answer: the team must fail over [by deleting its replication configuration], after which [the replica becomes writeable] (efs-replication-failover-delete-configuration-replica-writeable); it also needs mount targets, because EFS [does not create any mount targets] on the replica (efs-replication-destination-has-no-mount-targets).

sections.heading: The four FSx file systems match the storage and protocol you use today

plan.problem: Many companies already run a file server: Windows, NetApp, ZFS or a Lustre cluster. Amazon FSx gives each one a managed twin in AWS, so the applications keep their protocol and their features.
trace: **Start from today's system.** AWS maps Microsoft Windows Server to [FSx for Windows File Server] (fsx-when-to-choose-windows-from-windows-server), NetApp ONTAP or other NAS appliances to [FSx for NetApp ONTAP] (fsx-when-to-choose-ontap-from-nas), ZFS or other Linux file servers to [FSx for OpenZFS] (fsx-when-to-choose-openzfs-from-zfs), and Lustre or other parallel file systems to [FSx for Lustre] (fsx-when-to-choose-lustre-from-parallel-fs).
**Check the protocol.** FSx for OpenZFS serves [NFS 3, 4.0, 4.1, 4.2]; FSx for NetApp ONTAP adds SMB and iSCSI (fsx-compare-protocol-support).
**Check the clients.** FSx for Lustre lists [Linux] clients only (fsx-compare-client-compatibility); the other three serve Windows, Linux and macOS.
**Check the zones.** FSx for Lustre offers [Single-AZ - Persistent or Scratch]; the other three offer [Single-AZ and Multi-AZ] (fsx-compare-deployment-options).
plan.table: The four FSx types (columns: Question | Windows File Server | NetApp ONTAP | OpenZFS | Lustre; five columns are allowed in 2-deep.md): protocol | SMB | NFS, SMB, iSCSI | NFS | a custom POSIX-compliant protocol (fsx-compare-protocol-support); clients | Windows, Linux, macOS | Windows, Linux, macOS | Windows, Linux, macOS | [Linux] (fsx-compare-client-compatibility); deployment | Single-AZ or Multi-AZ | Single-AZ or Multi-AZ | Single-AZ or Multi-AZ | [Single-AZ - Persistent or Scratch] (fsx-compare-deployment-options); latency | [<1 ms] | [<1 ms] | [<0.5 ms] | [<1 ms] (fsx-compare-latency-by-type); Active Directory | yes | yes | no | no ([Active Directory support for file system access authentication], fsx-compare-active-directory-ontap-windows).
plan.why: Why four types? Each is one of the [four options that align to popular file systems] (fsx-decision-guide-four-file-systems-align-to-popular), so a migration keeps the application's protocol, permissions and tools; AWS points to FSx for applications that [run on network-attached file storage] (s3-files-vs-efs-vs-fsx; volatile, prose only).
plan.exam_signal: "move the file server without changing the application" points to the FSx type that matches today's server ([FSx for OpenZFS], fsx-when-to-choose-openzfs-from-zfs, and the other three rows of the same AWS table); "a shared file system for new Linux applications" points to Amazon EFS (subsection 1).
plan.diagram: efs-fsx-chooser (ladder), after the table; caption and alt fixed in diagrams below; no numbered steps.
plan.body_extras: Reference only: maximum throughput, size and IOPS per type (fsx-compare-max-*), SLA percentages (fsx-compare-availability-sla), compliance programs that are the same for all four (fsx-compare-compliance-all-four-types), Amazon File Cache (not taught).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: pick the FSx type that matches the file server you run today. The thing to watch is Lustre, which serves Linux clients.
plan.stop_and_answer: A company runs a NetApp filer that serves Linux over NFS and Windows over SMB from the same volumes. Which FSx type keeps that design? Answer: AWS recommends [FSx for NetApp ONTAP] for NetApp or other NAS appliances (fsx-when-to-choose-ontap-from-nas), and it gives [multi-protocol access] to the same data (fsx-faq-ontap-nfs-smb-multiprotocol).

sections.heading: FSx for Windows File Server serves SMB shares that join your Active Directory

plan.problem: A Windows file server holds shares, NTFS permissions and user sign-ins from Active Directory. Moving the files without those breaks every user's access.
trace: **Native Windows file servers.** FSx gives [fully managed Microsoft Windows file servers] with the [Server Message Block (SMB) protocol] (fsx-windows-fully-managed-native-windows-file-servers-smb).

**Join the domain.** When you create the file system, you [join it to your Active Directory domain] for [user authentication and file- and folder-level access control] (fsx-windows-joins-active-directory-for-authentication-and-acls): [AWS Managed Microsoft AD] or a [self-managed Microsoft AD] (fsx-faq-windows-active-directory-join).
**Keep the permissions.** FSx enforces [standard Windows access control lists (ACLs)], and existing ACLs migrate without changes (fsx-windows-bp-windows-acls-enforced-existing-acls-migrate).

**Move the data, keep the names.** AWS recommends DataSync, and [you can use Robust File Copy, or Robocopy] instead (fsx-windows-migrate-with-datasync-or-robocopy); DNS aliases let users [continue using the existing DNS names] (fsx-windows-dns-aliases-keep-existing-names).
plan.table: Which directory works (columns: Directory | Works with FSx for Windows File Server?): AWS Managed Microsoft AD | yes (fsx-windows-ad-options-aws-managed-or-self-managed); self-managed AD, on premises or on EC2 | yes, an [existing, self-managed Active Directory domain] (fsx-windows-ad-options-aws-managed-or-self-managed); AD Connector | no: [Amazon FSx does not support] it (fsx-windows-ad-connector-simple-ad-not-supported); Simple AD | no (same fact).
plan.why: Why Active Directory rather than IAM for users? SMB clients sign in with their domain identities, so FSx checks each domain user against the [Windows access control lists (ACLs)] of the files, while IAM policies control only the Amazon FSx API (fsx-windows-access-control-acls-security-groups-iam-ad).
plan.exam_signal: "SMB", "Windows file shares", "NTFS permissions" or "Active Directory users" points to FSx for Windows File Server ([join it to your Active Directory domain], fsx-windows-joins-active-directory-for-authentication-and-acls).
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: data in transit is [automatically encrypted using SMB Kerberos session keys] (fsx-windows-encrypted-in-transit-smb-kerberos-session-keys), and Linux clients mount the shares with [cifs-utils] (fsx-faq-windows-supported-windows-versions). Reference only: the resource-forest one-way trust, the domain-join service account, VPC sharing, Secrets Manager for the domain-join credentials (volatile), and Amazon FSx File Gateway, which is [no longer available to new customers] (fsx-windows-filegateway-closed-to-new-customers; chapter 25: <!-- xref: 25 Storage Gateway -->). Directory Service in depth is chapter 05 (<!-- xref: 05 AWS Managed Microsoft AD and AD Connector -->).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: FSx for Windows is a managed Windows file server in your domain. The thing to watch is the directory type.
plan.stop_and_answer: A company signs in to the AWS console through AD Connector. It wants FSx for Windows File Server to use the same on-premises domain. What must it do? Answer: join the file system to the on-premises domain as a self-managed AD, an [existing, self-managed Active Directory domain] (fsx-windows-ad-options-aws-managed-or-self-managed); [Amazon FSx does not support] AD Connector (fsx-windows-ad-connector-simple-ad-not-supported).

sections.heading: A Multi-AZ Windows file system fails over to a standby in another zone

plan.problem: A Single-AZ file system is one file server in one zone. If the server or the zone fails, users wait for recovery; production shares need a second server that is ready.
trace: **Two zones, one cluster.** A Multi-AZ file system runs across [a preferred AZ and a standby AZ] with [Windows Server Failover Clustering], and data is [replicated synchronously within each individual AZ] and between the two (fsx-windows-multi-az-standby-two-azs-sync-replication).

**Fail over automatically.** It fails over when [An Availability Zone outage occurs], when [The preferred file server becomes unavailable] or during planned maintenance (fsx-windows-failover-triggers-az-outage-unavailable-maintenance), in [less than 30 seconds] (fsx-windows-failover-under-30-seconds-failback-automatic).

**Same name for Windows.** The [DNS name remains the same], so failover is [transparent to Windows applications] (fsx-windows-failover-transparent-same-dns-name); Linux clients [do not support automatic DNS-based failover] (fsx-windows-linux-clients-no-automatic-dns-failover).
**Single-AZ waits.** Single-AZ has a [single Windows file server instance] and usually [about 30 minutes of downtime] during recovery (fsx-windows-single-az-one-server-one-az-30-minutes-downtime).
plan.table: Single-AZ or Multi-AZ (columns: Question | Single-AZ | Multi-AZ): file servers | a [single Windows file server instance] (fsx-windows-single-az-one-server-one-az-30-minutes-downtime) | a preferred and a standby server in two zones; failure of a zone | [about 30 minutes of downtime] for recovery | automatic failover in [less than 30 seconds] (fsx-windows-failover-under-30-seconds-failback-automatic); SQL Server shares | Single-AZ 2 can create CA shares | [use CA shares on Multi-AZ file systems] (fsx-windows-ca-shares-required-multi-az-for-sql-server); fits | [cost-efficient solution for test and development workloads] | [Multi-AZ file systems for most production workloads] (fsx-windows-multi-az-recommended-production-single-az-dev-test).
plan.why: Why put the standby in another zone? Multi-AZ gives [enhanced durability by further replicating data across AZs] and fails over by [failing over automatically to the standby AZ] (fsx-windows-multi-az-enhanced-durability-availability-auto-failover), so a zone outage leaves a complete copy ready.
plan.exam_signal: "Windows file shares must stay available if an Availability Zone fails" points to a Multi-AZ file system ([failing over automatically to the standby AZ], fsx-windows-multi-az-enhanced-durability-availability-auto-failover); "SQL Server failover cluster on SMB shares" points to Multi-AZ with continuously available shares ([continuously available (CA) file shares], fsx-windows-ca-shares-required-multi-az-for-sql-server).
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: you can test a failover by [modifying its throughput capacity] (fsx-windows-test-failover-by-changing-throughput-capacity), and after a failover, synchronizing can take [multiple hours for file systems with HDD] (fsx-windows-failover-io-paused-resync-hours-hdd). Reference only: failback times, SLA percentages, cross-zone access charges (volatile price facts), the feature table by deployment type (Single-AZ 1 is the type with DFS Replication).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Multi-AZ keeps a standby file server in a second zone. The thing to watch is Linux clients, which wait for failback.
plan.stop_and_answer: A Multi-AZ file system fails over during a zone outage. Windows users keep working, but a Linux report server that mounts the share with cifs-utils stops. Why, and when does it resume? Answer: Linux clients [do not support automatic DNS-based failover] (fsx-windows-linux-clients-no-automatic-dns-failover); they [resume file system operations] after the file system fails back to the preferred file server (same fact).

sections.heading: Windows file system storage grows in place but does not shrink

plan.problem: Unlike EFS, FSx for Windows File Server has a storage size that you choose. The team must plan the disk type, how the storage grows, and how users get old versions back.
trace: **Pick the disk.** SSD is for the [highest-performance and most latency-sensitive workloads], and HDD for [home directories, user and departmental shares] (fsx-windows-storage-hdd-vs-ssd-use-cases).

**Grow while in use.** You can increase storage and [increase or decrease the throughput capacity] while users work (fsx-faq-windows-increase-storage-change-throughput); a storage increase runs [without any downtime impact] (fsx-faq-windows-storage-grow-no-downtime).

**Never smaller.** Storage capacity is [Increase only] (fsx-windows-storage-capacity-increase-only-never-decrease), and the storage type changes only [from HDD to SSD] (fsx-windows-storage-type-hdd-to-ssd-only).

**Go past one file system.** DFS Namespaces group shares of several file systems into [one common folder structure, or namespace] (fsx-windows-dfs-namespaces-group-file-systems-scale-beyond-64-tib), beyond the [64 TiB] of one file system (fsx-windows-limit-max-storage-capacity).
plan.table: Changes after creation (columns: You want | Possible? | How): more storage | yes | update the storage, by a [minimum of 10 percent] each time (fsx-windows-storage-capacity-increase-minimum-10-percent); less storage | no: [Increase only] (fsx-windows-storage-capacity-increase-only-never-decrease) | move the data to a new, smaller file system with DataSync (fsx-windows-migrate-with-datasync-or-robocopy); HDD to SSD | yes: [from HDD to SSD] (fsx-windows-storage-type-hdd-to-ssd-only) | update the storage type; SSD to HDD | no ([from SSD to HDD], same fact) | restore a backup to a new HDD file system; more or less throughput | yes ([increase or decrease the throughput capacity], fsx-faq-windows-increase-storage-change-throughput) | update the throughput capacity.
plan.why: Why automate growth? Storage capacity is a setting that you provision and pay for (fsx-faq-windows-billing-dimensions), so a full file system needs an increase; AWS offers a [custom CloudFormation template] that increases it when free capacity [falls below a defined threshold] (fsx-windows-automatic-storage-increase-solution-cloudformation).
plan.exam_signal: "increase the storage automatically when free space is low" points to the AWS CloudFormation solution ([automatically increase your file system's storage capacity], fsx-windows-automatic-storage-increase-solution-cloudformation); "one share path for more data than one file system holds" points to DFS Namespaces ([one common folder structure, or namespace], fsx-windows-dfs-namespaces-group-file-systems-scale-beyond-64-tib).
plan.spot_the_bug: Spot the bug prompt: to cut cost, an administrator plans to change an SSD file system that holds home directories to HDD with one storage-type update, and later to lower its storage capacity. What is wrong? Reveal: the storage type changes only [from HDD to SSD], so going [from SSD to HDD] means restoring a backup to a new HDD file system (fsx-windows-storage-type-hdd-to-ssd-only), and storage capacity is [Increase only] (fsx-windows-storage-capacity-increase-only-never-decrease). About 60 words with the reveal; no sizes in the prompt (HDD has a minimum size).
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence each: backups are [file-system-consistent, highly durable, and incremental] (fsx-windows-backups-file-system-consistent-incremental-stored-in-s3), and user-initiated backups are [retained even after you delete the file system] (fsx-windows-user-initiated-backups-never-expire); shadow copies let users [quickly recover deleted or changed files] (fsx-windows-shadow-copy-definition-restore-previous-versions) but are [not a substitute for backups] (fsx-windows-shadow-copies-not-enabled-by-default-not-backup-substitute). Reference only: Data Deduplication savings ([50–60 percent for general-purpose file shares], fsx-windows-dedup-typical-savings-50-60-percent), 20 percent free space advice, minimum capacities, throughput and IOPS limits, the 6-hour wait between increases.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Windows storage grows while users keep working. The thing to watch is that it does not shrink, so start small.
plan.stop_and_answer: Home directories fill most of a 10 TiB file system, and the company expects 200 TiB under one share path within two years. What design scales? Answer: grow the storage now, each time by a [minimum of 10 percent] (fsx-windows-storage-capacity-increase-minimum-10-percent), and plan several file systems under DFS Namespaces, because one file system holds [64 TiB] (fsx-windows-limit-max-storage-capacity) and a namespace joins them into [one common folder structure, or namespace] (fsx-windows-dfs-namespaces-group-file-systems-scale-beyond-64-tib). The sizes are example values in the prompt.

sections.heading: FSx for Lustre feeds compute-heavy jobs and loads S3 data on first access

plan.problem: A training or simulation job reads a huge dataset in Amazon S3 many times. Expensive instances sit idle while data downloads, so the data must arrive as files at very high speed.
trace: **Built for speed.** FSx for Lustre serves [machine learning, high performance computing (HPC)] and [video processing, and financial modeling] (fsx-lustre-workloads-ml-hpc-video-financial), at [TB/s of throughput and millions of IOPS] (fsx-faq-lustre-tbps-millions-iops-sub-ms).

**Link a bucket.** A [data repository association (DRA)] links a directory to an S3 bucket or prefix (fsx-lustre-dra-links-directory-to-bucket-or-prefix), and the file system [transparently presents S3 objects as files] (fsx-lustre-s3-presents-objects-as-files-and-writes-back).

**Load on first read.** Content is [imported automatically from S3 only when you access] a file (fsx-faq-lustre-s3-object-imported-on-first-access), so jobs start while data is [lazy loaded as needed from Amazon S3] (fsx-lustre-lazy-loaded-from-s3-as-needed).

**Write results back.** The file system can [write file system data back to S3] (fsx-lustre-s3-presents-objects-as-files-and-writes-back), through automatic export or export tasks ([three types of data repository tasks], fsx-lustre-three-data-repository-task-types).

**Choose scratch or persistent.** On scratch, [Data is not replicated] (fsx-lustre-scratch-temporary-not-replicated); on persistent, [data is replicated] and [file servers are replaced if they fail] (fsx-lustre-persistent-replicated-servers-replaced).
plan.table: Scratch or persistent (columns: Question | Scratch | Persistent): built for | [cost-optimized storage for short-term, processing-heavy workloads] (fsx-lustre-use-scratch-for-short-term-persistent-for-long-term) | longer-term work that is [sensitive to disruptions in availability] (same fact); a file server fails | an [immediate I/O error] for the data on it (fsx-lustre-scratch-server-failure-io-error-no-replacement) | the server is [replaced automatically within minutes of failure] (fsx-lustre-persistent-failed-server-replaced-within-minutes-clients-retry); backups | none: [Backups aren’t supported on scratch file systems] (fsx-faq-lustre-backups-not-on-scratch) | yes, unless linked to S3 ([Backups aren’t supported on file systems linked], fsx-faq-lustre-backups-not-on-s3-linked). If the lint reads the curly-apostrophe contraction in these two displays as a contraction in prose (L803), request displays without it and report.
plan.why: Why load lazily? The bucket stays the long-term home of the data, and the file system holds only what jobs read; with SageMaker this means [eliminating the initial download step from Amazon S3] (fsx-lustre-sagemaker-input-source-skips-s3-download).
plan.exam_signal: "HPC", "machine learning training" or "data in S3 that a compute cluster reads at high throughput" points to FSx for Lustre linked to the bucket ([transparently presents S3 objects as files], fsx-lustre-s3-presents-objects-as-files-and-writes-back); "short-term" with "cost-optimized" points to scratch ([cost-optimized storage for short-term, processing-heavy workloads], fsx-lustre-use-scratch-for-short-term-persistent-for-long-term).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: data repository tasks and limits. A release task [retains the file listing and metadata] and [removes the local copy of that file's contents] (fsx-lustre-release-frees-space-keeps-metadata-reloads-from-s3). One file system takes a [maximum of 8 data repository associations] (fsx-lustre-dra-up-to-8-each-unique-directory-and-prefix), and several file systems can be [linked to the same S3 bucket] (fsx-faq-lustre-multiple-file-systems-one-bucket). Storage grows only: you [cannot decrease storage capacity] (fsx-lustre-storage-increase-only). Clients are Linux: [Linux-based AMIs] (fsx-lustre-clients-ec2-ecs-eks-linux-amis-lustre-client). At most 70 words.
plan.body_extras: Reference only: the Intelligent-Tiering storage class (change of 2025-05-29, volatile; it does not link to S3 data repositories), throughput per TiB, EFA, Spot Instance unmount advice, encryption at rest and in transit, AWS Batch and ParallelCluster.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: Lustre gives compute jobs fast file access to S3 data. The thing to watch is scratch, which keeps no replica.
plan.stop_and_answer: A team runs a two-week genome analysis on 300 TB in S3, reads each file once and writes results back to the bucket. If a server fails, the job can read the data from S3 again. Scratch or persistent? Answer: scratch, which is [cost-optimized storage for short-term, processing-heavy workloads] (fsx-lustre-use-scratch-for-short-term-persistent-for-long-term); the bucket keeps the data, so [Data is not replicated] (fsx-lustre-scratch-temporary-not-replicated) is acceptable. The values are example values in the prompt.

sections.heading: FSx for NetApp ONTAP serves NFS and SMB clients from the same data

plan.problem: Linux applications on NFS and Windows users on SMB often work on the same project data, usually on a NetApp filer. Two separate file systems would mean two copies and a sync job.
trace: **One copy, many protocols.** FSx for NetApp ONTAP gives [multi-protocol access] over NFS and SMB to the same data (fsx-faq-ontap-nfs-smb-multiprotocol), and block storage over the [iSCSI and NVMe-over-TCP protocols] (fsx-faq-ontap-iscsi-nvme-tcp-block).

**SVMs and volumes.** A storage virtual machine (SVM) is an [isolated file server] (fsx-faq-ontap-svm-isolated-file-server) that can [join SVMs to a Microsoft Active Directory] (fsx-ontap-svm-isolated-file-server-joins-active-directory); its volumes are [thin provisioned] (fsx-ontap-volumes-logical-containers-on-svms-thin-provisioned).

**SSD and capacity pool.** Data lives in [primary storage and capacity pool storage] (fsx-faq-ontap-two-storage-tiers); the capacity pool [can scale to petabytes in size] (fsx-faq-ontap-capacity-pool-elastic-petabytes).

**A policy per volume.** Each volume has a [tiering policy that controls whether data is moved] and a cooling period (fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-per-volume-cooling-period); Auto moves cold data after a cooling period that [by default is 31 days] (fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-auto-31-days-default-console).

**Replicate the NetApp way.** [NetApp SnapMirror replication] copies volumes to another FSx for ONTAP file system, also in another Region (fsx-faq-ontap-snapmirror-cross-region), with an RPO [as low as five minutes] (fsx-faq-ontap-snapmirror-rpo-5-minutes).
plan.table: Tiering policies (columns: Policy | What moves to capacity pool storage | Use it for): Auto | cold user data and snapshots (fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-auto-31-days-default-console) | volumes with a hot and a cold part; Snapshot Only | it [moves only snapshot data] (fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-snapshot-only-2-days-default-cli) | active data that must stay fast; All | it [marks all user data and snapshot data] as cold (fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-all-marks-everything-cold) | archive volumes; None | nothing: it [keeps all of your volume’s data] on SSD (fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-none-keeps-all-on-ssd) | latency-critical data.
plan.why: Why tier at all? You get SSD speed while paying for [SSD storage for only a small fraction] of the data (fsx-ontap-what-is-ssd-performance-pay-small-fraction), and in the capacity pool you [pay only for the storage space consumed] plus requests (fsx-ontap-pricing-capacity-pool-pay-for-consumed-plus-requests).
plan.exam_signal: "NetApp", "SnapMirror" or "NFS and SMB access to the same data" points to FSx for NetApp ONTAP ([multi-protocol access], fsx-faq-ontap-nfs-smb-multiprotocol); "WORM" or "SEC Rule 17a-4(f)" for file data points to SnapLock Compliance ([SEC Rule 17a-4(f)], fsx-faq-ontap-snaplock-compliance-use-case).
plan.go_deeper: Go deeper: SnapLock and Multi-AZ networking. SnapLock gives [write-once-read-many (WORM) protection] (fsx-faq-ontap-worm-snaplock); in Compliance mode a file [cannot be modified or deleted by any user] during its retention period (fsx-faq-ontap-snaplock-compliance-no-delete), while Enterprise lets authorized users [selectively delete WORM files or the SnapLock volume] (fsx-faq-ontap-snaplock-enterprise-flexible). Multi-AZ endpoints use floating IP addresses, so from outside the VPC you are [required to use Transit Gateway] (fsx-ontap-multi-az-outside-vpc-needs-transit-gateway). At most 70 words.
plan.body_extras: Reference only: FlexCache, storage efficiency ([65% from compression, deduplication, and compaction], fsx-ontap-storage-efficiency-65-percent-typical; typical), Autonomous Ransomware Protection (change of 2025-04-07, volatile), second-generation HA pairs, failover [typically within 60 seconds] (fsx-faq-ontap-failover-within-60-seconds; B-list), the VMware Cloud on AWS datastore, the deployment type that cannot change after creation. SnapLock licensing fees were removed on 2025-03-05 (volatile): do not teach a price.
plan.say_it: The short answer is: ONTAP serves NFS and SMB on one copy of the data. The thing to watch is each volume's tiering policy.
plan.stop_and_answer: A volume holds 50 TB of project files: 5 TB are edited this month, and the rest has not been opened for a year. Which tiering policy keeps the active files fast at the lowest cost? Answer: Auto, which moves cold user data and snapshots to capacity pool storage after the cooling period ([by default is 31 days], fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-auto-31-days-default-console); All would also move the active files ([marks all user data and snapshot data], fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-all-marks-everything-cold). The sizes are example values in the prompt.

sections.heading: FSx for OpenZFS moves ZFS and Linux NFS servers with snapshots and clones

plan.problem: Teams that run ZFS or Linux NFS servers depend on snapshots and fast clones for testing. They want the same tools in AWS without rewriting their scripts.
trace: **Same NFS, managed.** FSx for OpenZFS is a [fully managed file storage service] for data from [on-premises ZFS or other Linux-based file servers] (fsx-openzfs-fully-managed-move-from-onprem-zfs-linux-file-servers), reached over the [NFS protocol (v3, v4.0, v4.1, v4.2)] (fsx-openzfs-nfs-v3-v4-clients-linux-windows-macos).
**Snapshots.** A snapshot is a [read-only image of an FSx for OpenZFS volume] from which users [restore individual folders and files] (fsx-openzfs-snapshot-read-only-image-restore-files).

**Clones.** A clone is a [writable copy] [created almost instantly] from a snapshot, and you [cannot delete this source snapshot] while the clone uses it (fsx-openzfs-clone-volume-writable-instant-depends-on-snapshot).
**Low latency.** AWS lists [<0.5 ms] latency for FSx for OpenZFS (fsx-compare-latency-by-type).
**Choose availability.** It offers [Multi-AZ (HA), Single-AZ (HA), and Single-AZ (non-HA)] (fsx-openzfs-three-deployment-types-multi-az-single-az-ha-non-ha).
plan.table: Deployment types (columns: Type | After a failure | Fits): Multi-AZ (HA) | fails over to the other zone [typically within 60 seconds] (fsx-openzfs-multi-az-sync-two-azs-failover-60-seconds) | [business critical production workloads] (fsx-openzfs-multi-az-recommended-business-critical-database); Single-AZ (HA) | fails over to a standby in the same zone ([primary and standby file system within], fsx-openzfs-single-az-ha-primary-standby-same-az-60-seconds) | workloads that need [consistent single-AZ latencies] (fsx-faq-openzfs-single-az-ha-when); Single-AZ (non-HA) | [about 30 minutes of downtime] (fsx-openzfs-single-az-non-ha-cost-efficient-tolerates-downtime) | testing and development.
plan.why: Why clones? A clone starts from the snapshot's data, so it is [created almost instantly] (fsx-openzfs-clone-volume-writable-instant-depends-on-snapshot), while a [fully independent writable copy] takes a [significantly longer time to create] (fsx-openzfs-full-copy-volume-independent-slower).
plan.exam_signal: "ZFS", "Linux NFS file servers" or "snapshots and clones" points to FSx for OpenZFS ([on-premises ZFS or other Linux-based file servers], fsx-openzfs-fully-managed-move-from-onprem-zfs-linux-file-servers); "the lowest latency over NFS" points to OpenZFS ([<0.5 ms], fsx-compare-latency-by-type).
plan.body_extras: Only if words remain, one sentence: on-demand replication sends snapshots [within and across AWS Regions and accounts] (fsx-openzfs-on-demand-replication-snapshots-across-regions-accounts), for example to keep a [passive standby file system] (fsx-openzfs-replication-use-cases-read-replicas-passive-standby-dr). Reference only: the Intelligent-Tiering storage class (change of 2024-12-01, volatile), compression choices, S3 access points (volatile), quotas, backups with an [RTO of 5-10 minutes] (fsx-faq-openzfs-backups-pit-consistent-incremental-rto).
plan.say_it: The short answer is: OpenZFS moves ZFS servers with their snapshots and clones. The thing to watch is the deployment type you choose.
plan.stop_and_answer: A test team needs a fresh writable copy of a 20 TB production volume every morning, within minutes. A full copy takes hours. What do you create? Answer: a clone volume from the morning snapshot, a [writable copy] [created almost instantly] (fsx-openzfs-clone-volume-writable-instant-depends-on-snapshot); keep the snapshot while the clone exists. The 20 TB is an example value in the prompt.

traps.belief: Amazon EFS is a shared network file system, so Windows instances can mount it too.
traps.truth: Using Amazon EFS with Windows-based EC2 instances is not supported; Windows SMB shares belong on FSx for Windows File Server.

traps.belief: An EFS file system needs a storage size, and someone must grow it before it fills up.
traps.truth: Amazon EFS grows and shrinks automatically as files are added and removed; you provision no storage capacity.

traps.belief: You can turn on encryption at rest for an existing unencrypted EFS file system.
traps.truth: The encryption setting is fixed when the file system is created; create an encrypted file system and copy the data to it, for example with AWS DataSync.

traps.belief: Max I/O performance mode is the fastest EFS choice when many clients share a file system.
traps.truth: Max I/O has higher per-operation latency, and AWS recommends General Purpose mode; Max I/O is not supported for One Zone file systems or with Elastic throughput.

traps.belief: A scratch FSx for Lustre file system keeps its data safe when a file server fails, and you can back it up.
traps.truth: Scratch file systems do not replicate data and do not support backups; use a persistent file system for longer-term data.

traps.belief: An EFS One Zone file system stores data redundantly, so it survives the loss of its Availability Zone.
traps.truth: One Zone stores data redundantly inside one zone only; it is not resilient to a complete zone outage, and its data might be lost. A Regional file system is designed to sustain the loss of a zone.

traps.belief: For spiky, unpredictable throughput, provision EFS throughput for the peak.
traps.truth: Elastic throughput fits spiky or unpredictable workloads and charges for what you use; Provisioned throughput fits known, steady needs.

traps.belief: A file in EFS IA moves back to EFS Standard by itself when someone reads it.
traps.truth: By default, files stay in EFS IA or EFS Archive when they are read; set the Transition into Standard policy to move them back on first access.

traps.belief: An EFS replica in another Region accepts writes while replication runs, so both Regions can be active.
traps.truth: The destination file system is read-only while replication is enabled; to fail over, delete the replication configuration, and the replica becomes writeable.

traps.belief: FSx for Windows File Server can use AD Connector or Simple AD for its users.
traps.truth: Amazon FSx does not support AD Connector or Simple AD; join the file system to AWS Managed Microsoft AD or to a self-managed Active Directory.

traps.belief: A Single-AZ FSx for Windows File Server file system fails over to another Availability Zone when its zone fails.
traps.truth: A Single-AZ file system has one file server in one zone and usually about 30 minutes of downtime during recovery; only a Multi-AZ file system fails over to a standby file server in a second zone.

traps.belief: Linking FSx for Lustre to an S3 bucket copies the whole bucket into the file system before a job can start.
traps.truth: The file system presents the objects as files and imports an object's content only when the file is first accessed, so jobs start at once.

traps.belief: Linux NFS clients and Windows SMB clients that work on the same files need two file systems and a sync job.
traps.truth: FSx for NetApp ONTAP gives multi-protocol access: concurrent NFS and SMB access to the same data.

traps.belief: A file server that the team runs on EC2 instances is as little work as a managed file service.
traps.truth: On EC2 the team installs, patches, sizes and fails over the file server itself; Amazon EFS is serverless storage, and FSx gives fully managed file servers.
traps.placed_in: questions only (added by questions-23-1: efs-fsx-q001, efs-fsx-q006, efs-fsx-q017)

traps.belief: To get more throughput from an EFS file system on Bursting throughput, store extra data in it.
traps.truth: Bursting throughput scales with stored data, so padding pays for storage that nobody reads; Elastic or Provisioned throughput gives throughput without extra data.
traps.placed_in: questions only (added by questions-23-1: efs-fsx-q003, efs-fsx-q011)

traps.belief: An EFS client that encrypts its traffic connects to the mount target over HTTPS, so the security group needs a rule for port 443.
traps.truth: An NFS client can mount an EFS file system only if it can reach the NFS port (TCP port 2049) of a mount target; on-premises servers need an inbound rule for port 2049 in the mount target security group.

traps.belief: A shared file system is a good place for the data files of a database that runs on one instance.
traps.truth: Block storage is for low-latency, durable storage attached to single EC2 instances or containers, such as databases; file storage is for shared access from many instances.

traps.belief: Amazon EFS is the file system to choose for high-throughput machine learning or HPC jobs on a data set in Amazon S3.
traps.truth: FSx for Lustre is built for workloads where speed matters, such as machine learning and HPC, and a file system linked to S3 presents the objects as files and loads content on first access.

traps.belief: FSx for OpenZFS serves the same volumes to Linux clients over NFS and to Windows clients over SMB.
traps.truth: AWS lists NFS as the protocol of FSx for OpenZFS; concurrent NFS and SMB access to the same data is the multi-protocol access of FSx for NetApp ONTAP.

traps.belief: Amazon EFS is the answer for every migration of a Linux NFS file server, whatever storage system the company runs today.
traps.truth: AWS maps ZFS and other Linux-based file servers to FSx for OpenZFS, with snapshots and clones, and NetApp ONTAP or other NAS appliances to FSx for NetApp ONTAP.

traps.belief: One FSx for Windows File Server file system keeps growing for as long as the data grows.
traps.truth: A single SSD or HDD file system holds at most 64 TiB; Microsoft DFS Namespaces groups the shares of several file systems under one namespace to scale beyond that.

faq.q: Can on-premises servers and EC2 instances use the same EFS file system at the same time?
faq.answer: Yes; on premises and in the VPC together ([on-premises datacenter as well as EC2 instances])
faq.quote: You can access your Amazon EFS file system concurrently from servers in your on-premises datacenter as well as EC2 instances in your Amazon VPC.

faq.q: Can you keep data in EFS IA for a few days without a minimum duration charge?
faq.answer: Yes; EFS IA has [no minimum storage duration], but EFS Archive has one
faq.quote: EFS IA has no minimum storage duration. Data that is tiered to EFS Archive has a minimum storage duration of 90 days.

faq.q: Can tiny files in EFS IA cost less than a file of 128 KiB?
faq.answer: No; files [smaller than 128 KiB] are charged as 128 KiB
faq.quote: There is no minimum file size for IA or Archive, but files tiered to these storage classes that are smaller than 128 KiB will incur storage charges as if they were 128 KiB.

faq.q: Can you turn on encryption in transit without encryption at rest?
faq.answer: Yes; they are set [together or separately]
faq.quote: Encryption of data at rest and data in transit can be configured together or separately to help meet your unique security requirements.

faq.q: Can a Lambda function read and write files on EFS?
faq.answer: Yes; reference [an EFS file system in your function settings]
faq.quote: You can access EFS from functions running in Lambda by referencing an EFS file system in your function settings.

faq.q: Can one EFS file system hold more than a few terabytes?
faq.quote: You can store petabytes of data with Amazon EFS.

faq.q: Can you back up a scratch FSx for Lustre file system?
faq.answer: No; [Backups aren’t supported on scratch file systems]
faq.quote: Backups aren’t supported on scratch file systems because these file systems are designed for temporary storage and shorter-term processing of data.

faq.q: Can several FSx for Lustre file systems link to one S3 bucket?
faq.answer: Yes; many can be [linked to the same S3 bucket]
faq.quote: Yes, you can create multiple FSx for Lustre file systems linked to the same S3 bucket.

faq.q: Can Linux clients follow a Multi-AZ FSx for Windows File Server failover on their own?
faq.answer: No; they [don’t automatically connect to the standby file server] and resume after failback
faq.quote: Linux clients don’t automatically connect to the standby file server upon a failover, and will automatically resume file system operations once failback to the preferred file server is complete.

faq.q: Can you move all of a volume's data to capacity pool storage on FSx for NetApp ONTAP?
faq.answer: Yes; Amazon FSx [does not limit to the percentage] that you tier
faq.quote: Amazon FSx does not limit to the percentage of your data that you can tier to capacity pool storage.

decision_record.context: The trigger of data/startup.json chapter 23, at most 80 words, stage 2: the web tier runs on several instances in three Availability Zones behind the load balancer (availability_zones_used); a report created on one instance cannot be downloaded from another, because the download request often reaches another instance; conversion workers also need a shared work directory for the parts of long recordings that several workers convert (JSON note). decision_record.requirement: Report files and work files must be readable and writable from every web instance and every conversion worker in all three Availability Zones, with the LEAST change to the application (qualifier of the JSON: least change to the application).
options: sticky sessions, so that a user returns to the same instance

a shared Amazon EFS file system (chosen)
decision_record.decision: One Amazon EFS Regional file system, mounted by the web tier and by the conversion workers through a mount target in each of the three Availability Zones (data/startup.json choice), created encrypted, with Elastic throughput and a lifecycle policy that moves old reports to EFS IA (adds).
reasons_with_facts: Option 1: a sticky session can [bind a user's session to a specific target] (elb-alb-sticky-sessions-what), but the report still lives on one instance, and when the Auto Scaling group replaces an instance, [Data is not automatically copied] (ec2-auto-scaling-faq-data-not-copied-to-new-instances; lowercase the first letter in mid-sentence). The workers would still have no shared directory.

Option 2: Amazon S3 is reached through an [application programming interface (API) over the internet] (efs-decision-guide-object-storage-api-read-heavy), so the file code would have to change; the code cannot change this year (story, no AWS claim).

Option 3: EFS gives [shared read and write access] (efs-decision-guide-file-system-row-shared-access) to clients in every zone ([concurrently from multiple NFS clients], efs-concurrent-access-multiple-clients-multiple-azs) and [requires no changes to your existing applications] (efs-overview-regional-linux-shared-access); it grows [without provisioning or managing storage capacity] (efs-serverless-elastic-no-provisioning) and, as a Regional file system, stores data across [multiple geographically separated Availability Zones] (efs-regional-recommended-type). Each instance uses the mount target [within the same Availability Zone] (efs-regional-mount-target-per-az-same-az-access). Elastic throughput is [recommended for most use cases] (efs-elastic-throughput-default-recommended), and encryption at rest is chosen when the file system is created ([enable encryption at rest when creating], efs-two-forms-encryption-when-enabled).
