Keys: an EBS gp3 volume for the database instance ([attached to single Amazon EC2 instances or containers], efs-decision-guide-block-row-single-instance); one EFS Regional file system for the shared uploads ([shared read and write access], efs-decision-guide-file-system-row-shared-access). Distractors (five options): put the database files on the EFS file system (misconception: block storage fits databases; efs-faq-efs-vs-ebs-vs-s3); share the uploads on one EBS io2 Multi-Attach volume (trap ebs-trap-multi-attach-as-shared-file-system); keep the uploads on instance store volumes and copy them between instances (trap ebs-trap-instance-store-for-durable-data). Bullets also 3.1.K3, 2.1.K13.

qualifier 'none' (difficulty 1); the requirement is 'no capacity planning and no scaling work'. Linux instances share a data set that grows by an unpredictable amount each week; the team must never run out of space and does not want to size or grow storage. Which storage meets these requirements? Key: Amazon EFS ([without provisioning or managing storage capacity], efs-serverless-elastic-no-provisioning). Distractors: an EFS file system with a CloudWatch alarm and a Lambda function that raises its size (trap efs-fsx-trap-provision-capacity; impossible-feature: EFS has no size to raise; why links efs-faq-elastic-grow-shrink); FSx for OpenZFS with SSD storage sized for next year (violates-requirement: a size to plan; fsx-openzfs-two-storage-classes-intelligent-tiering-and-ssd); an EBS gp3 volume grown with Elastic Volumes (violates-requirement and sibling-confusion: one instance, manual growth). Bullets also 3.1.S2.

A research team trains machine learning models on a 200 TB dataset in an S3 bucket from a cluster of Linux GPU instances that needs very high file throughput. Training must start as soon as possible after the cluster launches, and results must end up in the bucket. LEAST operational overhead? Key: create an FSx for Lustre file system linked to the bucket with a data repository association and export results to it (fsx-lustre-s3-presents-objects-as-files-and-writes-back, fsx-faq-lustre-s3-object-imported-on-first-access). Distractors: create FSx for Lustre and first copy the whole bucket into it with AWS DataSync (trap efs-fsx-trap-lustre-copies-whole-bucket); copy the dataset to an EFS file system and mount it on every instance (violates-qualifier: a full copy before training; sibling-confusion); download the dataset to each instance's EBS volume at boot (violates-qualifier). Do not offer S3 Files as an option (volatile, and arguable). Bullets also 3.1.S1.

A company runs a short-lived HPC simulation for two weeks on input data in an S3 bucket; results go back to the bucket; if a file server fails, the job can read the input from S3 again. MOST cost-effective? Key: an FSx for Lustre scratch file system linked to the bucket (fsx-lustre-use-scratch-for-short-term-persistent-for-long-term). Distractors: a persistent file system with daily backups (violates-qualifier: replication and backups that the job does not need; fsx-lustre-persistent-replicated-servers-replaced); a scratch file system with daily backups to protect the results (trap efs-fsx-trap-lustre-scratch-keeps-data; impossible-feature, why links fsx-faq-lustre-backups-not-on-scratch); an EFS Regional file system with Provisioned throughput (sibling-confusion: not built for HPC throughput; fsx-decision-guide-lustre-speed-workloads). Think-aloud: six steps of STYLE 7, no wrong path. Bullets also 2.2.S8.

Production Windows file shares on FSx for Windows File Server must stay available to Windows users if an Availability Zone fails, with the LEAST operational overhead. Key: deploy a Multi-AZ file system (fsx-windows-multi-az-standby-two-azs-sync-replication, fsx-windows-multi-az-enhanced-durability-availability-auto-failover). Distractors: a Single-AZ 2 file system, which fails over to another zone on its own (trap efs-fsx-trap-single-az-fails-over; why links fsx-windows-single-az-one-server-one-az-30-minutes-downtime); two Single-AZ file systems in two zones kept in sync by a scheduled AWS DataSync task (violates-qualifier: a copy job and a manual switch; fsx-faq-windows-datasync-replicate-same-and-cross-region); a Single-AZ file system with daily backups restored in another zone after a failure (violates-requirement: hours of recovery). Bullets also 2.2.S8.

A company runs Microsoft SQL Server failover cluster instances on EC2 in two Availability Zones and needs shared storage on SMB for the database files, highly available across the zones and with the performance that a database needs. Which combination of steps meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead? (Select TWO.) Keys: create an FSx for Windows File Server Multi-AZ file system with SSD storage (fsx-windows-sql-server-ssd-recommended, fsx-windows-sql-server-active-data-files-or-share-witness-ssd); create continuously available (CA) file shares for the SQL Server files (fsx-windows-ca-shares-required-multi-az-for-sql-server). Distractors (five options): use an Amazon EFS file system for the database files (trap efs-fsx-trap-windows-clients); attach one EBS io2 Multi-Attach volume to the instances in both zones (trap ebs-trap-multi-attach-as-shared-file-system); choose HDD storage to lower the cost (violates-requirement: SSD is recommended for SQL Server). Bullets also 2.2.K11.

A company wants a lift-and-shift migration of an on-premises NetApp ONTAP file server to AWS. Linux applications use the data over NFS and Windows users over SMB, on the same volumes, and the team uses SnapMirror today. LEAST operational overhead? Key: migrate to FSx for NetApp ONTAP with NetApp SnapMirror and serve both protocols from the same volumes (fsx-faq-ontap-nfs-smb-multiprotocol, fsx-ontap-snapmirror-recommended-for-migrating-onprem-netapp). Distractors: Amazon EFS for the Linux data and FSx for Windows File Server for the Windows data, kept in sync by AWS DataSync (trap efs-fsx-trap-two-file-systems-for-nfs-and-smb); FSx for Windows File Server for both, with Linux clients on SMB (violates-requirement: the Linux applications use NFS; misconception); FSx for OpenZFS (sibling-confusion: NFS only, [NFS 3, 4.0, 4.1, 4.2], fsx-compare-protocol-support). Bullets also 2.2.S7.

An FSx for NetApp ONTAP volume holds 80 TB of engineering files. About 10% is edited every week and needs SSD latency; the rest is infrequently accessed. The volume was created with the AWS CLI and keeps its default policy. MOST cost-effective? Key: change the volume's tiering policy to Auto, so cold user data and snapshots move to capacity pool storage after the cooling period (fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-auto-31-days-default-console). Distractors: keep the default Snapshot Only policy (violates-qualifier: cold user data stays on SSD; fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-snapshot-only-2-days-default-cli); set the policy to All (violates-requirement: active files also move; fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-all-marks-everything-cold); set the policy to None and grow the SSD storage (violates-qualifier; fsx-ontap-tiering-policy-none-keeps-all-on-ssd). Never state a price. Bullets also 4.1.S10.

A company runs on-premises ZFS file servers that Linux applications use over NFS. Test teams create writable clones of production volumes from ZFS snapshots several times a day. The company wants to migrate without changing the applications or the snapshot and clone scripts' workflow, with the LEAST operational overhead. Key: FSx for OpenZFS (fsx-when-to-choose-openzfs-from-zfs, fsx-faq-openzfs-snapshots-clones-replication). Wrong path in the think-aloud: step 3 predicts 'Amazon EFS, because it is the shared NFS file system for Linux'; step 5: 'My first idea breaks because the stem asks to keep ZFS snapshots and writable clones, and AWS maps ZFS servers to FSx for OpenZFS.' Distractors: Amazon EFS with AWS Backup for copies (misconception: no ZFS clone workflow; violates-qualifier: restores instead of clones); FSx for NetApp ONTAP migrated with SnapMirror (wrong-configuration: SnapMirror replicates NetApp ONTAP systems, fsx-ontap-snapmirror-recommended-for-migrating-onprem-netapp); FSx for Lustre linked to S3 (sibling-confusion). Bullets also 2.2.S7, 3.1.S1.

A company keeps application files on an EFS file system in us-east-1. Disaster recovery requires an RPO and an RTO of minutes in us-west-2, with ongoing replication and the LEAST operational overhead. Which combination of steps meets these requirements? (Select TWO.) Keys: create an EFS Replication configuration with a destination file system in us-west-2 (efs-replication-destination-faq-region-or-az-of-choice, efs-replication-rpo-rto-minutes); during a disaster, delete the replication configuration so that the replica becomes writeable, and mount it in us-west-2 (efs-replication-failover-delete-configuration-replica-writeable). Distractors (five options): point the application in us-west-2 at the replica for writes while replication runs (trap efs-fsx-trap-replica-writable); copy daily AWS Backup recovery points to us-west-2 (violates-requirement: RPO of a day); run an hourly AWS DataSync task between the two file systems (violates-qualifier and requirement). Never let the 15-minute RPO decide the key (display pending fr-0098); the stable fact is 'RPO and RTO of minutes'. Bullets also 3.1.K2.

A company's Windows home directories on FSx for Windows File Server will grow to about 300 TiB in three years, and users must keep one share path. LEAST operational overhead? Key: create several FSx for Windows File Server file systems and group their shares under Microsoft DFS Namespaces (fsx-windows-dfs-namespaces-group-file-systems-scale-beyond-64-tib; one file system holds [64 TiB], fsx-windows-limit-max-storage-capacity). Distractors: keep one file system and increase its storage every quarter (violates-requirement: one file system holds 64 TiB); move the home directories to Amazon EFS, which grows without limits (trap efs-fsx-trap-windows-clients); store the files in Amazon S3 and map a drive with a third-party tool (violates-qualifier). Bullets also 4.1.S4.

speak.prompt: A volume, a file system or a bucket for these files: how do I decide?
speak.note: Ben's question of data/startup.json chapter 23 word for word. Short answer: it depends on who reads the files and how: one server needs a volume, many servers that read files need a file system, and an application that can call an API can use a bucket. How it works: a volume attaches to one instance in one zone; EFS is mounted by many Linux instances in every zone at once and needs no code change; Amazon S3 stores objects that the code reads and writes through an API. Watch: EFS serves Linux clients, not Windows, and file storage costs more than a bucket for data that nobody reads (story trade-off; keep it as Callvale's estimate, with no number). In your case: 'Can the code that writes the reports change this year, or must it keep writing to a directory?' Must not say: 'one EBS volume can be shared by all web servers'; 'S3 works like a disk without code changes'; 'EFS works for Windows servers too'.

speak.prompt: We are moving our Windows file server, with all its share permissions, to AWS. Can we just use EFS like our Linux team does?
speak.note: The prompt keeps the customer's 'just'; the model answer never uses it. Short answer: no, EFS does not serve Windows instances; FSx for Windows File Server is the managed Windows file server, with SMB shares and your Active Directory. How it works: the file system joins your domain, users sign in with their domain accounts, the Windows permissions move with the files, and DataSync or Robocopy copies the data while a DNS alias keeps the old share name. Watch: the directory must be AWS Managed Microsoft AD or your own Active Directory, not AD Connector. In your case: 'Where does your Active Directory run today, on premises or in AWS?' Must not say: 'EFS works on Windows with an NFS client'; 'you need to recreate all permissions'; 'AD Connector is enough for FSx'.

speak.persona: a machine learning founder in office hours
speak.prompt: Our training data is 200 terabytes in S3, and our GPUs wait on data. Should we copy everything to EFS first?
speak.note: First sentence starts 'Both': both are shared file systems that many instances mount, but they are built for different jobs. Short answer: no copy; link an FSx for Lustre file system to the bucket, so the files appear at once and load when first read. How it works: Lustre is built for machine learning and HPC throughput, lists the bucket's objects as files, pulls each file's content on first read and can write results back to the bucket. Watch: Lustre clients are Linux, and a scratch file system keeps no replica, so the bucket stays the safe copy. In your case: 'How long does one training run last, and can it read the data again from S3 if a server fails?' Must not say: 'Lustre copies the whole bucket first'; 'scratch file systems are backed up'; 'EFS is the fastest choice for GPU training'. Numbers as words: two hundred terabytes (prompt value).

speak.persona: a startup founder in office hours
speak.prompt: Our EFS bill grows every month, and most of the files are old. What can we do without touching the application?
speak.note: Short answer: turn on a lifecycle policy, so EFS moves files that nobody reads to cheaper storage classes on its own. How it works: new files land in EFS Standard; after thirty days without access a file moves to EFS Infrequent Access, which costs up to ninety-five percent less, and after ninety days to EFS Archive; the application sees the same paths. Watch: reading cold files costs a per-read charge and a slower first byte, Archive keeps a file for at least ninety days, and tiny files are billed as one hundred twenty-eight kibibytes; set 'move back on first access' if old files get busy again. In your case: 'How often does anyone open a file that is older than a month?' Must not say: 'the files move back to Standard by themselves'; 'IA is cheaper for every file'; 'you must change the application to use IA'. Spoken numbers from the fact cards' say forms when they exist.

diagrams.title: One file system, a mount target in each zone
diagrams.claim: Every instance reaches one shared file system through the mount target in its own Availability Zone.
diagrams.alt: Two Availability Zones in one Region. In each zone, an instance connects to the EFS mount target of its own zone. Both mount targets lead to one Amazon EFS file system, which stores the data across the zones.
say: Each instance mounts the file system by its Domain Name Service (DNS) name.
The name resolves to the IP address of the EFS mount target in the same zone.
The client connects to the NFS port (TCP port 2049) of that mount target.
The file system serves one to thousands of Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (EC2) instances at the same time.
A Regional file system stores data across multiple geographically separated Availability Zones.

diagrams.title: Which file service?
diagrams.claim: The clients, the protocol and the file server in use today decide which AWS file service fits.
diagrams.alt: A decision ladder with four questions. Windows clients with SMB and Active Directory lead to FSx for Windows. NetApp today, or NFS and SMB on the same data, lead to FSx for NetApp ONTAP. HPC or machine learning on S3 data leads to FSx for Lustre. A ZFS or Linux file server leads to FSx for OpenZFS. Everything else leads to Amazon EFS.
rungs: Windows clients, SMB and Active Directory? -> FSx for Windows
NetApp today, or NFS and SMB together? -> FSx for NetApp ONTAP
HPC or ML jobs on data in S3? -> FSx for Lustre
Moving ZFS or another Linux file server? -> FSx for OpenZFS
diagrams.note: Size s, four rungs and the else outcome; questions at most 9 words, outcomes at most 4 words; no numbers. The caption holds no absolute word and needs no link; it may link [four options that align to popular file systems] (fsx-decision-guide-four-file-systems-align-to-popular). The ladder order is a reading aid, not an AWS order: the table above carries the facts.
